The claimant has an interest in seeing that payment made.
The claimant, because of that interest, pays the money himself.
The claimant is entitled to be reimbursed by the person who was actually bound to pay.
breakdown.how_to_read: The "interest" requirement is the key gatekeeper — a stranger with no connection to the underlying obligation who volunteers to pay someone else's debt does not automatically get Section 69 reimbursement; the illustration's tenant-protecting-his-lease scenario is the textbook example of a genuine, legally-recognised interest that justifies the payment and the resulting right of recovery.

sections.title: Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act
sections.raw_text:
70. Obligation of person enjoying benefit of non-gratuitous act.—Where a person lawfully does anything for another person, or delivers anything to him, not intending to do so gratuitously, and such other person enjoys the benefit thereof, the latter is bound to make compensation to the former in respect of, or to restore, the thing so done or delivered.

Illustrations

(a) A, a tradesman, leaves goods at B's house by mistake. B treats the goods as his own. He is bound to pay A for them.

(b) A saves B's property from fire. A is not entitled to compensation from B, if the circumstances show that he intended to act gratuitously.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 70 is the broad, general quasi-contractual remedy against unjust enrichment: if someone lawfully does something for another, or delivers something to him, without intending it as a gift, and the recipient knowingly enjoys the benefit, the recipient must pay for it or return it — but there is no claim at all if the act was genuinely intended as gratuitous (illustration (b)).
essential_elements: A person lawfully does something for another, or delivers something to him.
He does not intend to act gratuitously (i.e. he expects payment or return).
The other person enjoys the benefit of that act or delivery, typically with knowledge of it.
The recipient is then bound to compensate for, or restore, the thing done or delivered.
exceptions_and_qualifications: No claim arises if the circumstances show the act was genuinely intended to be gratuitous (a true gift or volunteer act), as in illustration (b) — a person who saves another's burning property with no expectation of payment cannot later demand compensation.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 70 is one of the most frequently invoked quasi-contract provisions in Indian commercial litigation — e.g. for work done under a void or unenforceable contract that the other side nonetheless accepted the benefit of. Always establish, and plead, (i) non-gratuitous intention at the time of the act, and (ii) the recipient's knowing enjoyment of the benefit — both elements are independently required and are frequently contested at trial.

sections.title: Responsibility of finder of goods
sections.raw_text: 71. Responsibility of finder of goods.—A person who finds goods belonging to another, and takes them into his custody, is subject to the same responsibility as a bailee.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 71 treats a finder of lost goods who takes them into his custody as if he were a bailee (someone entrusted with another's property under Chapter IX of the Act) — meaning the finder owes the true owner the same duties of care, and has broadly the same rights (such as a lien for expenses), as a person who received the goods under an actual bailment contract.
essential_elements: A person finds goods belonging to another.
He takes those goods into his own custody.
He is then subject to the same duties and responsibilities as a bailee under the Act's bailment provisions.
breakdown.how_to_read: This short section is the bridge between the quasi-contract chapter and the bailment chapter (Sections 148-181) — once you establish someone is a "finder" under Section 71, go straight to the bailee provisions (duty of care under Section 151, the finder's specific rights under Sections 168-169) to work out his exact obligations and entitlements, rather than treating finding as a standalone regime.

sections.title: Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion
sections.raw_text:
72. Liability of person to whom money is paid, or thing delivered, by mistake or under coercion.—A person to whom money has been paid, or anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay or return it.

Illustrations

(a) A and B jointly owe 100 rupees to C. A alone pays the amount to C, and B, not knowing this fact, pays 100 rupees over again to C. C is bound to repay the amount to B.

(b) A railway company refuses to deliver up certain goods to the consignee, except upon the payment of an illegal charge for carriage. The consignee pays the sum charged in order to obtain the goods. He is entitled to recover so much of the charge as was illegally excessive.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 72 closes the quasi-contract chapter with the mistaken/coerced payment remedy: anyone who receives money or property because of the payer's mistake, or because the payer was coerced into paying, must give it back — including, per illustration (b), the illegally excessive portion of a charge extracted under commercial coercion (such as a carrier withholding goods pending an unlawful demand).
essential_elements: Money has been paid, or something delivered, to a person.
That payment or delivery was made by mistake, or under coercion.
The recipient must repay the money or return the thing.
breakdown.how_to_read: Illustration (b) is important beyond ordinary "mistake" cases — it shows Section 72 also reaches payments extracted through practical/commercial coercion (withholding goods pending an unlawful surcharge), not only coercion in the Section 15 sense; a party forced to pay an unlawful demand to secure delivery of goods can recover the illegal excess under this section even without proving the strict ingredients of Section 15 coercion.

sections.title: Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract
sections.raw_text:
73. Compensation for loss or damage caused by breach of contract.—When a contract has been broken, the party who suffers by such breach is entitled to receive, from the party who has broken the contract, compensation for any loss or damage caused to him thereby, which naturally arose in the usual course of things from such breach, or which the parties knew, when they made the contract, to be likely to result from the breach of it. Such compensation is not to be given for any remote and indirect loss or damage sustained by reason of the breach.

Compensation for failure to discharge obligation resembling those created by contract.—When an obligation resembling those created by contract has been incurred and has not been discharged, any person injured by the failure to discharge it is entitled to receive the same compensation from the party in default, as if such person had contracted to discharge it and had broken his contract.

Explanation.—In estimating the loss or damage arising from a breach of contract, the means which existed of remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance of the contract must be taken into account.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 73 is the Act's foundational damages provision, opening Chapter VI, "Of the Consequences of Breach of Contract." It entitles the innocent party to compensation for loss naturally arising from the breach in the ordinary course of things, or loss the parties actually contemplated as a likely result at the time of contracting — while expressly excluding remote and indirect loss. The Explanation adds a mitigation-style principle: the innocent party's available means of reducing his own loss must be factored into the damages calculation.
essential_elements: A contract has been broken.
The innocent party suffers loss or damage from the breach.
That loss must either (i) naturally arise in the usual course of things from the breach, or (ii) be loss the parties knew, at the time of contracting, was likely to result from the breach.
Remote and indirect loss is excluded from compensation altogether.
In estimating the loss, the means available to remedy/mitigate the inconvenience must be taken into account (the Explanation).
The same compensation principle applies to breach of quasi-contractual obligations (the second paragraph).
breakdown.how_to_read: This section codifies the same two-limb test as the English case Hadley v Baxendale (general/natural damages, and special damages within the parties' contemplation) — practitioners should organise pleadings around these two limbs specifically, and always address mitigation under the Explanation, since failing to mitigate reduces recoverable compensation. The eighteen illustrations to this section (not reproduced in the statutory text itself but published alongside it) are frequently cited in argument for analogous fact patterns — always locate the closest illustration to anchor a damages submission.

sections.title: Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for
sections.raw_text:
74. Compensation for breach of contract where penalty stipulated for.—When a contract has been broken, if a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach, or if the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the party complaining of the breach is entitled, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved to have been caused thereby, to receive from the party who has broken the contract reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or, as the case may be, the penalty stipulated for.

Explanation.—A stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a stipulation by way of penalty.

Exception.—When any person enters into any bail-bond, recognizance or other instrument of the same nature, or, under the provisions of any law, or under the orders of the Central Government or of any State Government, gives any bond for the performance of any public duty or act in which the public are interested, he shall be liable, upon breach of the condition of any such instrument, to pay the whole sum mentioned therein.

Explanation.—A person who enters into a contract with Government does not necessarily thereby undertake any public duty, or promise to do an act in which the public are interested.

Illustrations

(a) A contracts with B to pay B Rs. 1,000, if he fails to pay B Rs. 500 on a given day. A fails to pay B Rs. 500 on that day. B is entitled to recover from A such compensation, not exceeding Rs. 1,000, as the Court considers reasonable.

(b) A contracts with B that, if A practises as a surgeon within Calcutta, he will pay B Rs. 5,000. A practises as a surgeon in Calcutta. B is entitled to such compensation, not exceeding Rs. 5,000, as the Court considers reasonable.

(c) A gives a recognizance binding him in a penalty of Rs. 500 to appear in Court on a certain day. He forfeits his recognizance. He is liable to pay the whole penalty.

(d) A gives B a bond for the repayment of Rs. 1,000 with interest at 12 per cent. at the end of six months, with a stipulation that, in case of default, interest shall be payable at the rate of 75 per cent. from the date of default. This is a stipulation by way of penalty, and B is only entitled to recover from A such compensation as the Court considers reasonable.

(e) A, who owes money to B a money-lender, undertakes to repay him by delivering to him 10 maunds of grain on a certain date, and stipulates that, in the event of his not delivering the stipulated amount by the stipulated date, he shall be liable to deliver 20 maunds. This is a stipulation by way of penalty, and B is only entitled to reasonable compensation in case of breach.

(f) A undertakes to repay B a loan of Rs. 1,000 by five equal monthly instalments, with a stipulation that in default of payment of any instalment, the whole shall become due. This stipulation is not by way of penalty, and the contract may be enforced according to its terms.

(g) A borrows Rs. 100 from B and gives him a bond for Rs. 200 payable by five yearly instalments of Rs. 40, with a stipulation that, in default of payment of any instalment, the whole shall become due. This is a stipulation by way of penalty.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 74 is India's distinctive approach to liquidated-damages/penalty clauses — unlike English law's rigid liquidated-damages-vs-penalty distinction, Indian law treats every named sum or penalty stipulation the same way: the innocent party can recover reasonable compensation up to (but not exceeding) the stipulated amount, without needing to prove actual loss at all — the court has the power to scale the sum down to what is reasonable, but never to award more than what was stipulated.
essential_elements: A contract has been broken.
The contract names a sum payable on breach, or contains some other penalty stipulation.
The complaining party may recover reasonable compensation up to that named/stipulated amount — without needing to prove actual damage or loss.
The court determines what is "reasonable," capped at the stipulated figure.
exceptions_and_qualifications: The bail-bond/recognizance/public-duty-bond Exception: for these specific instruments, the whole sum named is recoverable, not merely reasonable compensation (illustration (c)).

A stipulation is not treated as a penalty at all if it merely accelerates an already-existing, non-penal obligation (illustration (f), where default simply advances the due date of instalments already owed) — contrast illustration (g), where the "acceleration" actually inflates the principal amount owed and is therefore struck down as a penalty.
breakdown.how_to_read: This is one of the most commercially significant sections in the entire Act (heavily litigated in construction, loan, and franchise disputes) — always distinguish a genuine acceleration clause (illustration (f), enforceable in full) from a disguised penalty dressed up as acceleration (illustration (g), capped at reasonable compensation); and remember a claimant under Section 74 need not lead evidence of actual loss to recover reasonable compensation, though evidence of actual loss helps persuade the court what "reasonable" means on the facts, and a complete absence of loss can still result in only nominal compensation being awarded.

sections.title: Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation
sections.raw_text:
75. Party rightfully rescinding contract, entitled to compensation.—A person who rightfully rescinds a contract is entitled to compensation for any damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

Illustration

A, a singer, contracts with B, the manager of a theatre, to sing at his theatre for two nights in every week during the next two months, and B engages to pay her 100 rupees for each night's performance. On the sixth night, A wilfully absents herself from the theatre, and B, in consequence, rescinds the contract. B is entitled to claim compensation for the damage which he has sustained through the non-fulfilment of the contract.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 75 closes the Consequences-of-Breach chapter by confirming that rescinding a contract rightfully (i.e. in response to the other party's breach, as under Section 39's repudiation rule) does not forfeit the innocent party's right to damages — he can rescind the contract AND still claim compensation for the loss the breach caused him, rather than having to choose one remedy to the exclusion of the other.
essential_elements: A party rightfully rescinds a contract — i.e. he had valid legal grounds to do so (such as the other party's breach/repudiation).
He is entitled to compensation for any damage sustained through the contract's non-fulfilment, in addition to the rescission itself.
breakdown.how_to_read: Section 75 should always be read together with Section 39 (repudiation gives the promisee an election to end the contract) and Section 73 (the general damages measure) — this section confirms that exercising the Section 39 election to terminate does not waive the Section 73 damages claim; both remedies are available together to the wronged party, as the singer illustration (mirrored from Section 39) makes explicit.
